methodological_rigor.justification: This is a retrospective single-center cohort of 86 patients with small pigmented choroidal lesions (29 melanomas, 57 nevi) comparing a manual risk score (MOLES) and an AI probability score (MelAInoma) against expert diagnosis (Methods 2.1–2.3; Results 3). The design is appropriate for assessing score agreement and association with diagnosis, and it uses prespecified trend testing, univariable/multivariable logistic regression including both predictors, and bootstrap internal validation plus sensitivity analysis by imaging modality (Results 3.2–3.8). Key limitations are the modest sample size, single-site setting, and a reference standard based on expert multimodal assessment without histopathology, with explicit risk of shared-feature incorporation because MOLES components overlap with clinician diagnostic criteria (Strengths and Limitations). Statistical execution is strong for the stated aims (ORs with CIs, model calibration checks, AIC comparison), but inference remains associative and needs external validation.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual retrospective cohort/diagnostic-association study, so Oxford LoE is best mapped to 2b (Methods 2.1–2.3). Clinical relevance is high because early discrimination of small choroidal melanoma from nevus affects referral, overtreatment, and metastatic risk, and the paper evaluates a reproducible photo-based AI tool intended for non-expert triage (Introduction; Abstract). The manuscript also clearly notes that clinical utility depends on thresholds and prospective real-world validation, which is not yet provided (Conclusions).

reporting_quality.justification: Given the diagnostic classification framing (melanoma vs. nevus) and comparison of two index tests against a reference classification, STARD is the most applicable reporting standard (Methods 2; Results 3; Strengths and Limitations). The manuscript reports cohort composition, inclusion/exclusion criteria, how each score was generated (including software version), and provides effect sizes with CIs plus calibration and internal validation elements (Methods 2.1–2.3; Results 3.1–3.8). The normalized text does not describe public release of images, labels, or executable model code, so reproducibility outside the center is limited.

novelty_literature.justification: The contribution is a head-to-head comparison showing that a single-photo AI output (MelAInoma) is only modestly correlated with MOLES yet remains independently associated with expert diagnosis when both are modeled together (R2 = 0.16 for correlation; multivariable ORs reported in Results 3.3 and 3.6). This is a meaningful but incremental advance in the growing space of AI-assisted ocular lesion triage, and the paper positions the AI as complementary rather than replacing multimodal assessment (Discussion/Conclusions). Stronger novelty would require external multicenter validation and explicit utility metrics at clinically chosen thresholds.

writing_presentation.justification: The abstract clearly states the clinical problem, the two tools, the cohort size and composition, and the main quantitative findings (monotonic trend; modest correlation; both predictors independently associated with diagnosis). Methods are concise and concrete about statistical tests (Jonckheere–Terpstra, linear regression, logistic regression, calibration) and the AI output definition (probability 0–1) (Methods 2.3). Limitations are explicitly discussed, including single-center design and lack of histopathology, which improves interpretability (Strengths and Limitations).

key_strengths: Directly clinically relevant triage question in a challenging setting (small lesions) with clear comparison of a manual multimodal score (MOLES) versus a reproducible photo-only AI score (MelAInoma).
Solid statistical analysis for association claims, including multivariable modeling with both predictors, calibration checks, and bootstrap internal validation (Results 3.6–3.8).

Transparent discussion of incorporation/shared-feature risk and the asymmetry of information available to MOLES vs. MelAInoma, improving interpretability of the comparison (Strengths and Limitations).
key_concerns: Single-center retrospective design with modest sample size limits generalizability; external multicenter validation is not provided (Strengths and Limitations; Conclusions).

Reference standard is expert clinical diagnosis without histopathology, and MOLES features overlap with clinician diagnostic criteria, creating potential incorporation bias (Strengths and Limitations).
No explicit data/code release for images and model execution is described in the normalized manuscript, limiting reproducibility.
chief_reviewer.rationale: The manuscript is well executed for an association/triage comparison study and could fit a tier-3 venue, but it needs major revisions focused on stronger validation framing and, ideally, external validation or clearer clinical-threshold utility analysis to support higher-tier claims.
